title: A Day at the Park
text: Anna goes to the park near her house every Sunday. She runs for twenty minutes and then sits under a big tree. Her brother brings sandwiches and orange juice. Birds come close because people often share their food. Anna feels calm before the busy week begins.

title: Learning to Cook
text: When Ken moved into his first apartment, he could not cook anything. He watched short videos and practiced one dish each weekend. At first he burned rice and used too much salt. Six months later, friends asked him to host dinners. Ken learned that small, regular practice beats sudden effort.

questions.question: How often did Ken practice?
questions.explanation: Ken practiced one dish each weekend.

questions.question: What happened after six months?
options: Friends asked him to host dinners
questions.explanation: The text says friends asked him to host dinners.

questions.question: What lesson does the passage teach?
options: Small regular practice beats sudden effort

title: The Night Market
text: Osaka's night markets glow with paper lanterns and the smell of grilled squid. Vendors shout prices while customers compare skewers. Tourists photograph everything, but locals simply eat and talk. A market lives longest when its regulars keep returning, not when its photos keep circulating.

title: Remote Work Revolution
text: Before 2020, commuting felt permanent. Then video calls replaced hallways, and kitchens became offices. Managers worried productivity would fall; several studies found it rose for focused tasks but fell for creative collaboration. The companies adapting best treat the office as a studio for teamwork, not a prison for attendance.

questions.explanation: The third sentence gives this contrast.

questions.question: How do adaptive companies view the office?
questions.explanation: Final sentence: as a studio for teamwork.

title: The Economics of Attention
text: Every app competes for the same scarce resource: human attention. Designers measure scroll depth and pause length the way factories once measured output per hour. Critics call this behavioural surplus extraction; defenders argue users freely trade attention for free services. Either way, the business model shapes what we notice, and what we notice shapes what we value.

questions.question: What do critics call the practice?
What is the author's concluding claim?
options: Business models shape attention and thus values

title: On Translation Loss
text: Translators joke that languages are polite conspiracies against directness. Japanese hedges with trailing verbs; Russian encodes aspect in the verb stem itself; English smuggles certainty into modal auxiliaries. A faithful translation therefore rarely reproduces words; it reconstructs intentions under foreign constraints, which is why two competent translators produce two defensible versions.

questions.explanation: Second sentence attributes hedging to Japanese.

questions.question: Why do two translators differ?
questions.explanation: Final sentence explains defensibility of multiple versions.
